source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. (1) Every rubric came back best-first; the program reads level 0 as the worst, so each question's rubric and the fit rubric were reversed. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. (2) per_dimension 1 -> 2, min_q 5 -> 8, max_q 8 -> 12, reserve_early 1 (unchanged): as written, coverage was met by the fourth answer and the budget ran to eight, so the judge chose almost nothing and `done` could not vary. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. (3) done_threshold 0.95 -> 0.5: the model's two attempts wrote 1 and then the bound's maximum, neither a considered number; 0.5 is the same provisional value the earlier 50-interview plan ran under. (4) Six questions added by the approver, written in the same style, so the pool exceeds the budget and some questions go unasked: two per technical dimension. A second generated draft failed validation twice and was not used. (5) ui text -> textarea, with text also allowed: these questions want prose. (6) One typo fixed in rust_readiness (聞かせます -> 聞かせてください). (7) done.true: 'at least once' -> 'at least twice', to match per_dimension. Nothing else was changed; dimension names and weights are the model's. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: My Java work has been fairly limited so far — mostly small services early in my one year here — so I haven't owned a transaction boundary decision myself. What I have spent most of my time on is a feature pipeline I built in Scala on Spark Structured Streaming for a fraud-scoring model, processing around 50TB of clickstream data a day. I replaced a 6-hour nightly batch job with a continuous streaming job that gets features to the model within a couple of seconds, and built a custom feature-versioning library in Scala that three other teams now depend on for reproducible training data.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience dealing with transaction boundaries in a production Java service at all. Even when asked for an example, only personal study or tutorial-level material comes up, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: I haven't done JVM or Kubernetes ops work on a Java service specifically. Most of my operational experience has actually been tuning Spark — getting executor memory and shuffle partition counts right on that same fraud-scoring pipeline so it didn't spill to disk under peak clickstream volume. I got shuffle spill down close to zero by repartitioning based on a key that distributed load more evenly across executors, and that's really been the bulk of my hands-on production tuning experience, on the data platform side rather than a Java backend.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience handling operational problems in a production environment. The answer stays at personal-project or study level, or drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: I haven't built idempotency handling in a payments context. The closest parallel in my own work is making the feature pipeline exactly-once — Spark Structured Streaming's checkpointing handles most of that, but I had to be careful with how I wrote the sink so a replayed micro-batch didn't double-count clickstream events, using the batch ID as a dedup key. That's the closest I can get to your question from my own experience so far.
answers.says: Can accurately explain idempotency and retry terminology and general techniques, but gives no real example of the implementation choices in their own system, or of noticing and recovering from a break. Nothing more concrete than ‘basically, we used an idempotency key,’ with no grounds for the decision or account of failure told as their own experience.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: I haven't operated an incident on a Java service. The pipeline had a rough day once, though — a Spark job failed for about three hours after an upstream schema change broke deserialization, and I ended up rewriting our schema validation to fail fast and alert instead of silently dropping malformed records, which is what had been happening before I noticed the drop in event counts. It's not the kind of incident you're asking about, but it's the closest thing I've been through.
answers.says: Describes an incident, but the timeline and numbers are vague; the account of cause and response is fluent, but the grounds for the decisions are not visible. The postmortem account is no more than ‘we did a retrospective,’ with no description of what actually changed or whether it worked. No sign of their own judgment about when or how to share the news.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't written Rust in production, and to be honest most of my energy this past year has gone into the Spark pipeline rather than exploring a new language. That pipeline is the thing I'm proudest of — it took our fraud model from features that were up to six hours stale to essentially real time, and the versioning library I wrote for it is now a small internal standard. I'd want to understand more about how a Rust migration would fit before I could give you a real plan for it.
answers.says: Has barely touched Rust and has no realistic outlook for learning it. Says they're ‘willing to learn,’ but cannot give a concrete plan for where to start or how long it would take to become production-ready. Cannot speak to boundary design for migration either.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: I don't have a strong view on where to cut a ledger boundary for Rust — that's not something I've worked close to. The closest thing I've done to a boundary decision was separating the raw ingestion layer from the feature-computation layer in the Spark pipeline, so the two could scale independently, which is part of why it handles 50TB a day without the feature logic being coupled to how the raw events arrive. It's a similar idea, I think, just in a different stack than what you're asking about.
answers.says: Has no experience making boundary-design or migration decisions themselves, and even when pressed, gives nothing beyond reciting general principles. Cannot construct a concrete plan of their own for where to start.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I flagged the schema-validation gap in the pipeline the same day I found it, in our team channel, rather than sitting on it. I don't have real on-call experience on a backend service, but I do a kind of informal rotation for the data pipeline, and I've helped two other teams debug issues with the feature-versioning library I wrote, which has been a nice way to see how it's used elsewhere.
answers.says: Says they have experience sharing mistakes and doing on-call, but with no specifics — no more than ‘I reported it normally’ or ‘I did take on-call shifts’ — with no sign of their own judgment or effort. On mentoring juniors, they've never given it thought, or cannot describe any experience.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: I haven't had a real production emergency on a backend service. The closest thing was pushing a fix to the Spark job during that three-hour outage — I did get someone to glance at the diff first even though it was late, mostly out of habit from how careful we try to be with the feature pipeline given how many models depend on it downstream.
answers.says: On skipping the procedure in an emergency, says in general terms that ‘the principle should be upheld,’ but has no real example of being forced to make that call themselves, and the answer stays theoretical. Or the answer stays at ‘it depends on the situation,’ without giving concrete criteria for where they personally would draw the line. Technically correct understanding, but with no experience behind it.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: I haven't restored data consistency in a production Java service. The nearest thing is fixing duplicate feature rows in the pipeline's output table after that schema-change incident — I wrote a dedup query keyed on event ID and batch timestamp, reran the backfill for the affected three-hour window, and checked row counts against the raw event log to confirm it matched afterward.
answers.says: Names a concrete inconsistency in a production service they were responsible for (e.g., double counting, a missing journal entry, a batch job that stopped partway), and describes how they scoped the impact (query, count, time period), how they fixed it (a correcting record rather than an overwrite, a backfill), and how they verified the fix afterward (reconciliation, recalculation), with numbers. Can also describe it if their first read of the problem was wrong.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you improved latency or throughput in a production Java service based on measurement. Give me the before-and-after numbers, and if you tried something that didn't work, tell me that too.
answers.answer: No Java performance work from me. The performance story I do have is the Spark pipeline again — cutting end-to-end feature latency from about six hours to under two seconds by moving from batch to streaming, and separately getting shuffle spill down to near zero through repartitioning, which I mentioned earlier. I tried increasing executor count first as a quick fix for the spill issue and it didn't help at all, since the actual problem was data skew, not raw capacity.
answers.says: Cannot describe any production performance-improvement experience at all. Stays at personal-project level, or drifts into unrelated talk.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I disagreed with a teammate who wanted to switch our feature pipeline from Spark Structured Streaming to a simpler batch job for cost reasons. I benchmarked both and showed the model's accuracy actually dropped measurably with six-hour-stale features versus near-real-time ones, using a week of held-out fraud labels, and we kept streaming. That's the clearest example I have of arguing a technical decision with data, even if it's not a Java or money example.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: I've written a little Rust outside of work — I started rewriting a small command-line log parser I originally had in Python, mostly to see what the fuss was about. I got stuck fighting the borrow checker trying to hold a reference into a line while also pushing parsed records into a Vec, and ended up just cloning the string instead of fighting it further, which isn't elegant but got me unstuck. It's a small side thing next to the Spark work, honestly.
answers.says: Names concretely what failed to compile in their own code (e.g., a borrow conflict, a lifetime annotation, a Send/Sync constraint, a tokio runtime boundary), how they fixed it, and how they came to understand the fix, in their own words. If it was production work, which part of production it was comes out concretely; if personal, what they built comes out concretely.

fit.says: The candidate is broadly aligned with most of the working principles, but shows a conditional attitude in some areas — for example, saying something to the effect of ‘in an emergency, you should fix it first even if it means skipping the procedure,’ without committing to announcing and recording that skip, or not speaking positively about on-call or support work. They could work here, but some coaching would be needed to bring them fully in line with the principles.
